title: Multi-step word problems and estimation
blurb: Solve one- and two-step money, rate, supply and dosage word problems at exam pace, and estimate to check the answer.
question: A nursing assistant earns $18.50 an hour and works 32 hours. From that pay she covers rent of $425, groceries of $96.40 and gas of $54.75. How much is left, and how do you avoid stopping one step short?

teach.body: Formally, a multi-step problem needs two or more operations, where the result of one step feeds the next. In plain English: the answer is at the end of a short chain, and the HESI A2 puts the links of that chain (the intermediate values) among the wrong options. At about a minute per item, work to a plan: know exactly what is asked, in which units, before you compute.

steps.label: Read the last line
steps.sub: what is asked, in what units?

teach.h: Worked example: change from a purchase
items: Asked: the CHANGE from $50 after buying 5 boxes of gauze at $4.85 and 4 bottles of saline at $2.35.
Estimate: 5 × 5 + 4 × 2.5 = 35, so about $15 change. ✓ The total, $33.65, is an intermediate value, not the answer.

teach.h: Worked examples: unit price and rate
items: Better buy: 18 oz for $4.32 or 28 oz for $6.44? Unit prices: 4.32 ÷ 18 = $0.24/oz; 6.44 ÷ 28 = $0.23/oz. The 28 oz size is cheaper per ounce.
Rate: 150 miles in 2.5 hours. Speed = distance ÷ time = 150 ÷ 2.5 = 60 mph.
Units guide the operation: miles ÷ hours = miles per hour.

head: Strategy
How
Example
teach.caption: Rounding both numbers UP overestimates; rounding both DOWN underestimates.

teach.h: When context overrides the rounding rule
teach.caption: Here the normal rule would give 4 buses (too few) and 7 items (can't afford).
The bars add back to the paycheck: 425 + 96.40 + 54.75 + 15.85 = 592.

teach.text: The word-problem traps: stopping at an intermediate value (the subtotal, the amount used); answering "how many more" with a total; mixing units (minutes with hours, cents with dollars); and rounding a count the wrong way (round up for "how many boxes needed," down for "how many full doses").

teach.body: Tyrone Jackson, a nursing assistant saving for nursing school, earns $18.50 an hour for 32 hours: 18.50 × 32 = $592.00. Bills: 425 + 96.40 + 54.75 = $576.15. Left: 592.00 − 576.15 = $15.85. Estimate: 18 × 32 ≈ 580 and bills ≈ 425 + 100 + 55 = 580, so a small amount left is reasonable. ✓

items: Read the last line first: what is asked, and in what units?
Write each step's result with its unit; the last step answers the question.
Estimate with compatible numbers to catch a misplaced point or a wrong operation.
Round up for "enough," down for "complete units."

summary: You can now solve one- and two-step money, rate, supply and dosage problems: read what is asked, chain the operations, keep units straight and check the result. You also estimate quickly and spot the intermediate-value and wrong-rounding options the HESI A2 plants.

A.q: During a shift a patient drank 240 mL of juice, 1 1/2 cups of water and 180 mL of broth. Use 1 cup = 240 mL. What was the patient's total intake in milliliters?

whyNot.1: 660 counts the water as 1 cup (240 mL) instead of 1 1/2 cups.
whyNot.3: 600 leaves out the 180 mL of broth.

A.q: A clinic orders 49 cases of gloves at $31.75 per case. Rounding each number to the nearest ten, which is the best estimate of the total cost?
A.why: 49 rounds to 50 and $31.75 rounds to $30. Estimate: 50 × $30 = $1,500. (Exact: $1,555.75.)

whyNot.1: $1,200 rounds 49 down to 40; the ones digit 9 means rounding up.
whyNot.2: $1,600 rounds $31.75 to the nearest dollar ($32), not the nearest ten.
whyNot.3: $2,000 rounds $31.75 up to $40; the ones digit 1 means rounding down.

A.q: A bottle holds 90 tablets. A patient takes 1 1/2 tablets three times a day. How many days will the bottle last?

whyNot.0: 30 divides by the 3 doses but leaves out that each dose is 1 1/2 tablets.
whyNot.2: 60 divides by one dose (1.5) instead of the daily amount (4.5).

B.q: Isabella has $150. She buys 3 sets of scrubs at $24.95 each and a pair of shoes for $38.50. How much money does she have left?

whyNot.0: $86.55 subtracts the price of one set of scrubs instead of three.
whyNot.1: $113.35 is the amount spent, an intermediate value; the question asks what is left.

B.q: An ambulance travels 18 miles at an average speed of 45 miles per hour. How many minutes does the trip take?
B.why: Time = distance ÷ speed = 18 ÷ 45 = 0.4 hour. Convert: 0.4 × 60 = 24 minutes.

whyNot.1: 40 min reads 0.4 hour as 40 minutes; an hour has 60 minutes, so 0.4 h = 24 min.
whyNot.2: 2.5 divides speed by distance (45 ÷ 18); time is distance ÷ speed.
whyNot.3: 810 multiplies distance by speed; d = r × t means t = d ÷ r.

B.q: A nurse gave 3 doses of 125 mg in the morning and 2 doses of 250 mg in the evening. How many more milligrams were given in the evening than in the morning?
B.why: Morning: 3 × 125 = 375 mg. Evening: 2 × 250 = 500 mg. Difference: 500 − 375 = 125 mg.

whyNot.0: 875 mg is the total for the day; "how many more" asks for a difference.
whyNot.1: 500 mg is the evening total, an intermediate value.
whyNot.3: 375 mg is the morning total, an intermediate value.

C.q: A 1,200 mL bag of fluid infuses at 80 mL per hour for 6.5 hours. How much fluid is left in the bag?

whyNot.0: 520 mL is the amount infused, not the amount left.
whyNot.1: 640 mL rounds the time up to 7 hours (80 × 7 = 560).
whyNot.2: 720 mL uses 6 hours and drops the half hour (80 × 6 = 480).

C.q: A unit needs 1,150 alcohol pads for the month and has 175 on hand. Pads come in boxes of 200. How many boxes must be ordered?
C.why: Still needed: 1,150 − 175 = 975 pads. Boxes: 975 ÷ 200 = 4.875. The unit needs enough, so round up: 5 boxes (1,000 pads).

whyNot.0: 4 boxes rounds 4.875 down; 800 + 175 = 975 pads is 175 short.
whyNot.2: 6 boxes leaves out the 175 pads on hand (1,150 ÷ 200 = 5.75, rounded up).
whyNot.3: 7 boxes adds the pads on hand to the need instead of subtracting them (1,325 ÷ 200 = 6.6).

C.q: A patient uses 2 puffs of an inhaler twice a day. Each inhaler holds 200 puffs. How many full weeks will one inhaler last?
C.why: Per day: 2 × 2 = 4 puffs. Days: 200 ÷ 4 = 50. Weeks: 50 ÷ 7 = 7.14, and only full weeks count, so 7.

whyNot.0: 8 rounds 7.14 up, but the inhaler runs out partway through the 8th week.
whyNot.1: 50 is the number of days, an intermediate value; the question asks for weeks.
whyNot.3: 14 counts 2 puffs a day instead of 4 (200 ÷ 2 = 100 days ÷ 7).

reteach.title: A word problem is a road trip
reteach.question: You drive 42 miles at 56 mph to a clinical placement, then 18 miles at 36 mph to a second site. How long is the whole trip, and why can't you jump straight to the destination?

blocks.h: Each leg ends where the next begins
blocks.body: A GPS doesn't teleport you: it plans legs. Leg 1 turns distance and speed into time: 42 ÷ 56 = 0.75 h = 45 min. Leg 2: 18 ÷ 36 = 0.5 h = 30 min. Only then do you add: 45 + 30 = 75 min = 1 h 15 min. Each leg's time is a waypoint, not the destination. On the HESI A2, waypoints appear as wrong options to catch anyone who stops early.

items: Reasonable? 60 miles at roughly 50 mph is a little over an hour. ✓
Averaging the speeds ((56 + 36) ÷ 2 = 46 mph) and dividing 60 miles by it gives 78 minutes: close, but wrong, because the legs take different times.

blocks.text: 0.75 hour is 45 minutes, not 75 minutes. Convert decimal hours by multiplying by 60.

explain.body: Underline what is asked. "How many more" and "how much is left" are differences, not totals. Every value you compute on the way is a possible wrong option.

test.q: A clinic has 480 flu shots. It gives 135 on Monday and 162 on Tuesday. How many more shots must it give to use all of them?
test.why: Given so far: 135 + 162 = 297. Still to give: 480 − 297 = 183. Check: 297 + 183 = 480.

whyNot.1: 297 is the number already given, an intermediate value.
whyNot.2: 27 is the difference between Monday and Tuesday, not what remains.
whyNot.3: 777 adds every number in the problem.

explain.body: Round each number to one that is easy to work with, usually one nonzero digit, then compute in your head. Use the estimate to rule out options with a misplaced point.

test.q: Which is the best estimate of 7.9 × 51.2?
test.why: 7.9 is close to 8 and 51.2 is close to 50: 8 × 50 = 400. (Exact: 404.48.)

whyNot.0: 350 truncates 7.9 to 7 instead of rounding it to 8.
whyNot.1: 480 rounds 51.2 up to 60; to the nearest ten it is 50.
whyNot.3: 4,000 has the decimal point one place too far right.

explain.body: A rate is one quantity per one unit of another. Let the units decide: miles ÷ hours gives miles per hour. 15 minutes is 1/4 hour, so scale up by 4.

test.q: A patient in cardiac rehab walks 0.6 mile in 15 minutes. At this rate, what is the patient's speed in miles per hour?
test.why: 15 minutes = 1/4 hour, so in 1 hour: 0.6 × 4 = 2.4 miles. Speed = 2.4 mph.

whyNot.0: 0.04 is miles per MINUTE (0.6 ÷ 15), an intermediate value.
whyNot.1: 9 multiplies 0.6 × 15 instead of converting to hours.
whyNot.2: 25 divides 15 by 0.6, which gives minutes per mile, not miles per hour.

explain.body: Find the total coming in, find the total going out, then subtract. Line up decimal points and keep cents.

test.q: Jamal earns $16.25 an hour and works 24 hours. He pays $45.50 for a textbook and $112 for a uniform. How much of his pay is left?

whyNot.0: $390.00 is his pay before costs, an intermediate value.
